git: the minimal setup that keeps me safe

The problem it solves

Without version control the project is a folder of files called final, final_v2 and final_really. You cannot see what changed, you cannot go back, you cannot try an idea without risking the working version, and you cannot share the work with anyone. With coding agents editing files it gets worse, because they change a lot of files quickly.

The general idea

git stores snapshots of the whole project, called commits, with a message each. Branches let you try an idea on the side and merge it when it works, and a remote such as GitHub keeps a copy and shares the work. The idea is simple. The habits around it are what keep it simple.

Examples

git init
git add -- analysis.py README.md
git commit -m "Add the loader"

git switch -c feature          # try an idea on a branch
git commit -m "Try a new model"
git switch main
git merge feature

gh repo create my-project --private --source . --remote origin --push

Tips from my setup

  • Minimal git, in writing. My global agent instructions say: when the task is finished, run the checks and commit only the files you changed with git add -- <files>. No branches, stash, reset, clean, rebase, amend or push unless I ask, and never stage unrelated files. The history stays readable even when an agent does the typing. See the post about my Claude setup.
  • A global gitignore. One file keeps the things that never belong in git out of every repository: data/, *.env, logs, zip files, caches and the folders of my coding agents. Data goes to DVC instead.
  • Recipes for the boring parts. just create makes a private GitHub repository from the current folder, sets the remote and pushes, and just clone clones one of mine. See the post about just.
  • lazygit for everything interactive. Staging single hunks, amending and resolving conflicts are faster in lazygit than in the command line. See the post about TUIs.
  • Imperative commit messages, one change per commit, and a commit at the end of every finished task.

Expert things

Branches

A branch is a cheap label on a commit. I use one for every idea that might fail: a new model, a refactor, an experiment with a different data source. If it works I merge it, if it does not I delete the branch and main never knew. With agents the rule is stricter: the agent works on a branch, I review the diff, and only then does it reach main.

git switch -c try-new-model
git log --oneline --graph --all
git branch -d try-new-model     # the idea did not work

Worktrees

A worktree checks out another branch into a second folder that shares the same repository. You can run a long job on one branch while you edit on another, or give each agent its own folder so that two of them never overwrite each other's files. No stashing, no half-finished changes in the way.

git worktree add ../project-feature feature
git worktree list
git worktree remove ../project-feature

Notes

A commit message cannot be edited without rewriting history, but a note can. git notes attaches extra text to a commit without changing it. I use it for things I learn later: which run of the pipeline used this commit, what the result was, why a change was reverted.

git notes add -m "AUC 0.81 on the 2021 sample" HEAD
git log --show-notes

DVC for the data

git is bad at big files and data does not belong in it. DVC keeps a small pointer file in git and the data itself in a remote, so one commit describes the code and the exact data it ran on. Going back to an old commit means going back to the old data as well.

Why the agent should commit after every modification

  • Every step is a restore point. If the next edit breaks something, one git restore or git revert undoes exactly that step instead of an hour of mixed changes.
  • The diff stays reviewable. Ten small commits are easy to read. One huge change at the end is not, and that is where mistakes slip through.
  • Agents drift. A long session loses track of what it changed. The history is the record of what actually happened, not what the agent remembers.
  • Bisecting works. When a bug appears later, git bisect finds the commit that caused it, but only if the commits are small.
  • Parallel agents need it. With worktrees and several agents, small commits make merging painless.
